title: Reverse engineering Orrery: solving the five-planet serial
summary: Working through Orrery's hidden 8x8 planet grid, probe physics, custom serial format, and an AI-assisted solver that turns the survey into a valid serial.

blocks.text: Running `orrery.exe` without arguments prints a telescope survey instead of asking for a serial immediately.
I used `ORRERY_DAY` to keep the challenge on a fixed day while solving it:
The program prints 32 probe results. Each probe can be absorbed, reflected, or deflected to another edge coordinate.

A quick note before getting into it: this write-up was AI-assisted. I used AI to help translate the harder parts of the Binary Ninja decompilation, check my understanding of the probe simulation, and verify the solver. I still stepped through the binary and tested the final serial myself.

The challenge description says that five planets are hidden somewhere inside an 8x8 grid. The program does not store the planet positions directly. Instead, it stores the results that probes would produce.
The probes are ordered like this:

blocks.label: snippet.txt
blocks.value:
top edge:       (1,0) through (8,0)
left/right:     (0,1), (9,1), (0,2), (9,2), ...
bottom edge:    (1,9) through (8,9)

blocks.text: The program uses a 10x10 grid. The outside border is made up of coordinates 0 and 9, while the planets can only be placed between them.
A ray starts on the border and moves into the grid.
The important rules are:

blocks.label: snippet.txt

blocks.text: The program stores the result as a number:
For example, a ray that exits through (6,9) is stored as:
The serial is exactly eight characters long. It uses this custom alphabet:
The program uses `strchr` to find each serial character inside that alphabet. The difference between the returned pointer and the start of the alphabet gives the character's numeric value.
Each character contributes five bits:
Eight characters give us 40 bits in total.
The lowest 10 bits are a checksum. The remaining 30 bits contain the actual data:
The checksum uses FNV-1a:

blocks.label: snippet.c

blocks.text: Only the lowest 10 bits of the resulting hash are compared with the checksum from the serial.
The name is also involved in the serial.
The program first trims whitespace and converts the name to uppercase. It then hashes the name with FNV-1a and keeps the lowest 30 bits:
The payload is combined with this name hash:
This gives five six-bit values. Each value represents one position in the 8x8 interior grid:
For the layout I found, the five values were:
Those values correspond to:
So the planets are located at:
There are only 64 possible interior cells, and the challenge uses five planets:
That is large enough that doing it manually would be annoying, but small enough to brute-force with a script.
I copied the probe behaviour into Python and compared every possible layout against the survey table:

blocks.label: keygen.py

blocks.text: The matching layout was:
After finding the layout, I generated a serial for the name `TEST`.
For this name:

blocks.label: snippet.txt
blocks.value:
name hash  = 0x32d739e5
planet data = 0x000420ca
payload     = 0x32d3192f
checksum    = 0x0b0

blocks.text: Packing the payload and checksum together produces:
Converting that value through the custom alphabet gives:
Running it against the original binary:
produces:
The final fingerprint is also calculated with FNV-1a. It uses the five sorted planet values followed by the four little-endian bytes of the name hash:
This is why the name matters. Changing the name changes both the serial and the final fingerprint.
The final survey comparison happens here:

blocks.label: snippet.asm
blocks.value:
0x1400030ac    call    memcmp
0x1400030b1    test    eax, eax
0x1400030b5    jne     0x140003169

blocks.text: memcmp returns zero when the simulated probe results match the table. The `jne` branch goes to the failure message when the result is not zero.

It would be possible to patch this branch and force execution into the fingerprint code. However, the program still calculates the final value from the decoded planet data and the name hash afterwards.

So skipping the comparison does not produce a proper solution. The useful approach here is writing a small keygen that reconstructs the planets from the survey and then creates a valid serial for the chosen name.

title: Soulreaper_shell crackme
summary: Taking apart a small x86-64 shell crackme in Binary Ninja, recovering REAPER42 with Python, then inverting the branch that enforces the key check.

blocks.text: Running `soulreaper_shell` normally reveals a small shell with its own prompt.

blocks.alt: The soulreaper shell showing its prompt and accepting regular shell commands.

blocks.text: You can execute regular commands as if this were a normal shell. Commands such as `mkdir`, `cat`, and `nano` are passed to the system and work as long as they are available in the environment.
I didn't find any obvious commands or other attack vectors that could be used to crack the program, so I opened it in Binary Ninja.

The decompiled `main` function first calls `sub_401610`. If that function returns a non-zero value, the program prints `Debugger Detected` and stops processing commands. I didn't reverse this function because it isn't needed to recover the key or patch the password check.

There are also a few lines involving `fsbase + 0x28`. These are stack-canary checks added by the compiler. The function saves a value from that location when it starts, then compares it again before returning. If the values are different, the program assumes that something overwrote part of the stack and calls `__stack_chk_fail`.
That code is protection against stack corruption. It is not part of the key check.
After the anti-debugging check, the program repeatedly prints its prompt and reads a line of input. It removes the newline, splits the line into arguments, and looks at the first argument.
The relevant logic is roughly:

blocks.label: snippet.c

blocks.text: So `reap` is a custom command. Its first argument is passed to `sub_401560`, which is the function that checks the key.
The important part of `sub_401560` is:

blocks.label: snippet.c

blocks.text: The first thing it does is check that the argument is exactly 8 characters long. It then transforms each input byte by XORing it with `0x2a` and adding an increment that starts at `7` and increases by `3` each time.
The increments used for the eight characters are:

One confusing part of the Binary Ninja output is that it shows `var_18` as an `int64_t` and `correct` as an `int64_t*`. That makes it look as if the function is comparing 64-bit values, but the logic is actually working with the eight individual bytes stored in that value. When the decompiler's types look strange, the assembly is more reliable than the generated C-like output.
Since x86-64 uses little-endian byte order, the bytes of the constant are stored as:
The check is:
To reverse it, we undo the addition first and then undo the XOR:
I copied the inverse transformation into a short Python script:

blocks.label: snippet.python
blocks.value:
value = 0x34378e828a78797f
expected = value.to_bytes(8, byteorder="little")

password = bytearray()
increment = 7

for stored_byte in expected:
    character = ((stored_byte - increment) ^ 0x2a) & 0xff
    password.append(character)
    increment += 3

print("Password:", password.decode())

blocks.text: This gives:
Using it as the argument to `reap` gives the success message:

blocks.label: snippet.txt
blocks.value:
soulreaper shell > reap REAPER42
Access granted
join us : https://t.me/+blTRfHi8oKJiN2E0

blocks.alt: The soulreaper shell accepting REAPER42 and printing Access granted.

blocks.text: Recovering the password is one way to solve the challenge. Another way is to change the conditional branch that decides whether the validator result is accepted.
The relevant assembly in `main` is:

blocks.label: snippet.asm
blocks.value:
0x401390  call sub_401560
0x401395  test eax, eax
0x401397  je   0x4013f8

0x401399  lea  rsi, [rel data_402061]  ; "Access granted"
0x4013a0  mov  edi, 0x2
0x4013a5  xor  eax, eax
0x4013a7  call __printf_chk

blocks.text: The return value from `sub_401560` is placed in `eax`. The `test eax, eax` instruction checks whether that value is zero:

blocks.label: snippet.txt
blocks.value:
eax = 0  -> zero flag is set -> invalid key
eax = 1  -> zero flag is clear -> valid key

blocks.text: The original `je` means “jump if equal to zero”. Therefore, when the validator returns `0`, execution jumps to the `Access denied` block at `0x4013f8`. When the validator returns `1`, execution falls through to the granted block at `0x401399`.
I used Binary Ninja's invert-branch patch on the instruction at `0x401397`, changing `je` to `jne`.
The original and patched bytes are:
After the patch, an invalid key no longer jumps to the denied block. It falls through to the granted block instead:

blocks.label: snippet.txt
blocks.value:
eax = 0  -> jne is not taken -> Access granted
eax = 1  -> jne is taken     -> Access denied

blocks.text: The `reap` command still needs an argument, because the null-argument check happens before the validator is called. However, any key that fails the original check can now reach the success path.

blocks.alt: The patched soulreaper shell accepting an invalid key and printing Access granted.

title: First Post - what_password crackme
summary: Taking apart a small x86-64 crackme in Binary Ninja, recovering its password with Python, then patching the check so any input works.

blocks.text: Running `what_password` doesn't print a prompt. It just waits for input, then prints `Incorrect password!` if the guess is wrong.

blocks.alt: Terminal showing the what_password crackme rejecting several incorrect password guesses.

blocks.text: I opened the binary in Binary Ninja and jumped to `main`. It's a 64-bit x86 ELF, and the symbols haven't been stripped, so there isn't much hunting around to do.
`main` starts by reading up to `0x400` bytes from stdin into `input`.
After that, `r14` is initialized to `0` and `r15` to `2`. In the loop, `r14` is the index into the password data and `r15` is a value added to each decoded byte.
Each byte from `pw` is XORed with `0x27`, then the current increment is added. The result is compared against the corresponding byte from our input.
In simplified form, the check looks like this:

blocks.label: Simplified password check

blocks.text: So there's no need to brute-force anything. The binary already contains everything needed to reconstruct the expected input.
`pw` starts at `0x404028`:
I copied the transformation into a short Python script:

blocks.label: solve.py
blocks.value:
stored_bytes = bytes.fromhex(
    "4e 49 1d 42 7c 41 7c 33 75 6a 6b 3c 7e 7f cb"
)

password = bytearray()
increment = 2

for stored_byte in stored_bytes:
    expected = ((stored_byte ^ 0x27) + increment) & 0xff
    password.append(expected)

    if expected == 0x0a:
        break

    increment += 2

print(bytes(password))

blocks.text: Which gives:
The final `\n` is the newline from pressing Enter, so the actual password is:

blocks.alt: Terminal showing the recovered password being accepted by the original crackme.

blocks.text: Recovering the password is one way to solve it. The easier way, if all you care about is reaching the success path, is to patch the conditional branch.

blocks.alt: Binary Ninja graph view of main showing the comparison loop and the wrong and right branches.

blocks.text: The relevant instructions are:

blocks.label: Original control flow
blocks.value:
cmp r12b, r13b
jne wrong
cmp r12b, 0x0a
je right

blocks.text: At `0x401199`, the `jne 0x4011b0` sends execution to the failure path when the bytes don't match.
I replaced it with an unconditional jump to the success block at `0x4011d5`:

blocks.label: Patched control flow
blocks.value:
cmp r12b, r13b
jmp right
nop

blocks.text: The original conditional jump was only two bytes, while the replacement `jmp` is five, so Binary Ninja overwrote the following bytes as well and padded the remainder with a `nop`.
With that patch in place, the comparison no longer matters. Any input reaches the `Correct! You won!` branch.

blocks.alt: Terminal showing the patched crackme accepting a one-character input.
